title: The Death of Socrates
notes: p3.3: the lettered bubble 'That is how we know.' stays; voice_speech changes Plato's spoken line, because Plato was not present (Phaedo 59b). Optional patch: re-letter the bubble as 'I was ill. They told me.'

p2.1, p2.3, p2.4: the kneeling, weeping friend in the gold-trimmed cloak is drawn like Plato on p3.3. Narration names him Crito (who made the escape offer). Optional patch: change the cloak so he does not read as Plato.
p1.4: caption 'Five hundred and one citizens found him guilty' overstates: a majority did (Apology 36a). Narration corrects it ('most did').
p3.2: Socrates' last words are voice only; no bubble is lettered.
p3.4: the archaeologists hold what looks like a glass bottle; the finds were small clay medicine bottles. Narration says clay. Low priority.
p2.4: narration is under 12 words on purpose (climax: let the SFX play).

panels.visual: Socrates (ugly, bald, bushy beard, barefoot, shabby cloak) in the Agora cheerfully asking a puzzled merchant questions, question marks flying
panels.caption: In 399 BC, Socrates asked awkward questions.
panels.narr: This barefoot old man is Socrates. For years he wandered this Agora asking awkward questions. The poor man on the right only wanted to sell a pot.

voice_speech.speaker: Socrates
voice_speech.text: But what is justice? You must know, surely?

panels.visual: Grumpy Athenians in a crowd with arms folded glaring at Socrates, angry shadows
panels.caption: People did not always like the answers.
panels.narr: People did not always like the answers. Socrates showed important men, in public, that they didn't know what they thought they knew. Important men remember that.

panels.visual: A courtroom of 501 jurors in rows, shown as a vast crowd of faces, Socrates standing alone in the centre
panels.caption: He was accused of disrespecting the gods and corrupting the young.
panels.narr: In 399 BC they took him to court. He was accused of disrespecting the gods and corrupting the young. Five hundred and one jurors. One old man, alone in the middle.

panels.visual: A juror's black pebble dropped in an urn, closer view, tension, Socrates' calm face in the background
panels.caption: Five hundred and one citizens found him guilty.
panels.narr: Each juror dropped a pebble. Not all of them voted guilty, but most did: if about thirty had changed their minds, he'd have gone home. Look at his face. Calm.

panels.visual: Socrates in a prison cell with a small barred window and a stone bed, his friends (Crito, a grey-haired man in a plain brown cloak, and two young men; no one in a gold-trimmed cloak) kneeling beside him urging him to leave
panels.caption: His friends offered to help him escape.
panels.narr: His friends offered to help him escape. Crito, his old friend, came to the prison before dawn. The money was ready. Friends far away would hide him.

panels.visual: Close-up of Socrates shaking his head with a kind smile, the old friend Crito's hand on his shoulder
panels.caption: He refused them.
panels.narr: He refused them. All his life he had lived by the laws of Athens. He wasn't going to sneak out of them now, by the back door.

voice_speech.speaker: Socrates
voice_speech.text: I will stay. After seventy years, should I run now, Crito?

panels.visual: A servant carrying a clay cup of hemlock on a tray into the cell, grim faces
panels.caption: The sentence was death by poison: hemlock.
panels.narr: The sentence was death by poison: hemlock, made from a plant. A man carried it in. Even the prison guard had cried when he came to say goodbye.

panels.visual: Socrates calmly raising the clay cup, eyes serene above the rim, friends weeping behind him, a small '...'
panels.caption: He drank the cup calmly.
panels.narr: He drank the cup calmly. All of it.

panels.visual: Socrates lying on the bed still talking and gesturing to his friends, who listen in tears
panels.caption: He went on talking about philosophy.
panels.narr: All day he had talked about philosophy with his friends, as if it were any other afternoon. After the cup, he walked about until his legs grew heavy. Then he lay down.

panels.visual: His legs under a blanket, a dimming curve of grey shading creeping up from his feet
panels.caption: The numbness crept up his body.
panels.narr: Socrates couldn't feel his feet when the man pressed them. The numbness crept up his body. His last words were for Crito, about Asclepius, the god of healing.

voice_speech.speaker: Socrates
voice_speech.text: Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Pay it, won't you?

panels.visual: Young Plato, pale and ill, wrapped in a blanket in a chair at home, writing at a table with a quill and a papyrus by a warm lamp, later, a friend telling him the news
panels.caption: Plato was ill and not there. He wrote it down afterwards.

speech.speaker: Plato
speech.text: I was ill. They told me.

panels.narr: Then he was still. Plato wrote down what happened that day. But Plato wasn't there: he was ill. His friends told him everything.

voice_speech.speaker: Plato
voice_speech.text: I was ill that day. My friends told me everything.

panels.visual: The Agora building in the south-west corner (small, dusty), archaeologists holding up a tiny clay medicine bottle, a big question mark above
panels.caption: It may have been the prison. Nobody can prove it.
panels.narr: That's history: it happened, and here's how we know: Plato. The prison is a best guess: a building in the south-west corner where diggers found tiny clay medicine bottles. Go and find it.
